sections.title: Paris events
sections.content:
• Tonight: a free urban-history walk along rue Nationale. The Comité d’histoire de la Ville de Paris meets at Métro Place d’Italie today, 5 August, for a guided walk from 18:00 to 20:00. The route follows the 13th arrondissement street from its former ragpickers’ settlements and semi-rural edges through the clearance and rebuilding of the Deux-Moulins area. It is free, but limited to 25 people and requires advance booking. Official listing and registration

  • Léna Aubert with Lola Payen and Giampolo Missaglia — Thursday 6 August. 38Riv Jazz Club, 38 rue de Rivoli, Paris 4e; 21:30–22:30; €21–24 online / €24–27 on site. The unusual bass-and-two-voice/guitar formation is centred on composed melody, vocal texture and intimate ensemble colour rather than an extended jam, making it the more focused jazz option this week. Event and booking

  • Zeta at Supersonic — Friday 7 August. Supersonic, 9 rue Biscornet, Paris 12e; doors 19:00, Zeta listed at 22:30; free entry. The Venezuelan-founded group builds post-rock around dense Afro-Caribbean polyrhythm, punk force and psychedelic guitar atmosphere. This is the high-energy alternative to the seated jazz programme, and the percussion-first construction is more distinctive than a generic post-rock crescendo. Official listing

sections.title: CS and AI developments
sections.content:
PAST-Bench tests whether a personal agent actually learns across fresh sessions

A personal agent can appear to improve over time while merely receiving a longer prompt or retrieving a convenient old answer. PAST-Bench tries to separate those effects by evaluating agents across 26 scenarios and 204 episodes in which useful experience must survive into later, fresh-session tasks. The benchmark isolates four operations: saving relevant experience, retrieving it when needed, reusing procedures, and replacing information that has become obsolete.

The important design choice is the counterfactual comparison: run the same later task with retained experience enabled and disabled. Two systems can show the same aggregate gain while failing for different reasons—one may never store the right state, while another stores it but retrieves the wrong memory. The authors’ interventions improve average performance, especially when old state must be overwritten, but the results remain model-dependent. The broader systems point is useful: “memory” should be tested as a sequence of inspectable state transitions, not as a single end-to-end score. Paper

StreamDAM treats object disappearance as a memory-control problem

Most video-object-segmentation systems are evaluated offline: they may process every frame eventually, even if computation falls behind the camera. StreamDAM instead imposes an honest 30 fps deadline; if the model misses a frame, the application must display a stale mask. Under that constraint, a tracker’s memory policy becomes as important as its segmentation quality.

The proposed system learns a compact presence signal and uses it to control when memory is written, how far back the tracker reads, when it should withhold an output, and when it should attempt re-detection. A fixed rule fails because occlusion and genuine disappearance demand opposite behaviour: during occlusion, old identity evidence should be preserved; after disappearance, continually writing background into memory corrupts the target representation. The paper is a new preprint, so its claimed lead still needs independent replication, but it identifies the right abstraction: real-time perception is partly a cache-coherence problem under deadlines. Paper

sections.title: Technical idea: BBR estimates the network path instead of waiting for packet loss
sections.content:
Traditional TCP congestion control treats packet loss as evidence that the sender is transmitting too quickly. That proxy worked reasonably well when routers had small buffers, but modern paths break the equivalence. A deep buffer can absorb packets while adding seconds of queueing delay—bufferbloat—whereas a shallow or wireless link may drop packets even though substantial capacity remains unused.

BBR—Bottleneck Bandwidth and Round-trip propagation time—builds an explicit model from acknowledgements:

  • estimate the maximum recent delivery rate, approximately the bottleneck bandwidth;
  • estimate the minimum recent round-trip time, approximately propagation delay without a queue;
  • multiply them to obtain the path’s bandwidth-delay product, the amount of data needed in flight to keep the pipe full;
  • pace sending near the estimated bandwidth and constrain in-flight data near the estimated pipe size.

The two estimates interfere with each other. You cannot observe the minimum RTT while maintaining a standing queue, and you cannot know whether more bandwidth is available without briefly sending faster. BBR therefore cycles through states: rapid startup, queue draining, periodic bandwidth probes and occasional low-inflight RTT probes. Current BBRv3 also incorporates loss and fairness controls; the IETF specification is still an experimental draft rather than a finished standard.

The general lesson extends beyond networking: when a feedback signal is only an accidental proxy for the latent variable you care about, model the latent system and deliberately probe it. Original BBR paper · March 2026 IETF BBRv3 draft

sections.title: Non-CS science: an accidental lunar impact becomes a calibration experiment
sections.content:
At about 06:35 UTC today, a discarded Falcon 9 upper stage weighing roughly four tonnes was expected—and is now believed—to have struck the far western edge of the Moon at about 2.4 km/s. Telescopes did not immediately confirm the flash because the predicted site lies close to the lunar limb, so the impact should still be described as highly expected rather than directly observed. NASA plans to look for before-and-after imagery.

Unlike an unknown natural meteoroid, this object had a reconstructed launch history, estimated mass, measured spectrum and tracked rotation. That turns the collision into a useful calibration point: researchers can compare a reasonably well-characterised projectile with the resulting crater, ejecta curtain and any detectable seismic signal. The same data can improve estimates of how impact energy couples into lunar soil and how far dust travels—questions that matter for the placement of future habitats, instruments and landing sites.

There is no danger to Earth. The practical warning is about cislunar traffic management: hardware sent beyond low Earth orbit may remain on chaotic trajectories for years, and today’s accidental experiment is also evidence that disposal plans must account for the Moon as infrastructure accumulates around it. Impact report · Observational-planning paper · Physical-characterisation paper

sections.title: Geopolitics and political economy
sections.content:
• Iran and the Strait of Hormuz: U.S.–Iran negotiations produced talk of an interim arrangement, mediated with Oman, to restore shipping through the strait. Oil fell and equities rose on the expectation, but Tehran says a wider agreement remains blocked while U.S. threats continue. The distinction matters: reopening a transport chokepoint would reduce the immediate oil shock without resolving the war’s political causes. Reuters

  • The war is becoming a munitions constraint: Reuters sources say the United States has used virtually all available ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles allocated across its global stockpile and somewhat under half its Tomahawks during five months of war. The White House disputes any readiness problem, and exact inventories are classified, but the mechanism is clear: long-range stand-off weapons substitute capital-intensive missiles for riskier piloted sorties, so a prolonged campaign transfers pressure from the battlefield to production lead times and commitments in Europe and Asia. Reuters

  • Russia–North Korea: Ukrainian intelligence says a roughly 90-person North Korean missile unit is deploying to Russia’s Voronezh region and could eventually operate with 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers. Reuters could not independently verify the claim. If confirmed, this would move cooperation beyond weapons transfer toward personnel embedded in an operational strike system, while exploiting Ukraine’s shortage of Patriot-class interceptors. Reuters

  • Myanmar: a resistance umbrella body has publicly committed to pursuing a negotiated political solution, while Thailand and the Philippines are pressing both sides toward contact. The junta has not accepted the group as a negotiating partner and has regained battlefield ground, so the near-term development is only talk about talks. Diplomacy is emerging partly because the balance of force changed, not because the underlying conflict over military rule was resolved. Reuters

  • France’s climate-budget feedback loop: repeated heatwaves and wildfires are estimated to impose €3–6 billion in 2026 costs, complicating an already narrow deficit-reduction plan. The fiscal effect is not limited to emergency spending: agricultural losses, insurance claims, constrained electricity output and lower labour productivity all reduce revenue or raise costs at once. Climate adaptation is therefore becoming an annual budget-capacity question rather than an exceptional environmental line item. Le Monde

sections.title: Marxist fragment
sections.content:
“It is a pre-eminent means for the realisation of surplus value; it is in itself a province of accumulation.”

— Rosa Luxemburg, The Accumulation of Capital, Chapter 32, “Militarism as a Province of Accumulation.” Primary text

Luxemburg is not claiming that weapons create social wealth merely by being destructive. Her argument concerns effective demand and class power. Taxation transfers purchasing power to the state, which becomes a concentrated and predictable buyer of armaments; capital receives a protected market whose scale is politically determined rather than limited by workers’ consumption.

That mechanism is visible in the current munitions problem. Depleted inventories generate pressure for multi-year procurement, new factories and guaranteed orders. The state socializes demand risk while private firms retain the production contracts. Luxemburg’s wider accumulation theory is contested, but this narrower observation remains useful: militarism is simultaneously coercive policy and an institutional market-making device.

sections.title: Two philosophy and political fragments
sections.content:
Adam Smith: property security produces an asymmetric political coalition

“Men of inferior wealth combine to defend those of superior wealth in the possession of their property.”

— Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, Book V, Chapter I, Part II, “Of the Expense of Justice.” Primary text

Smith’s point is more structural than the caricature of government as simply hired by the richest person. Small proprietors support an order that protects large fortunes because the same legal apparatus also protects their lesser holdings. The coalition is mutually intelligible but asymmetric: everyone receives formal property security, while those with the most property receive the greatest absolute protection. This helps explain why institutions can command broad consent while reproducing a highly unequal distribution.

Max Weber: politics demands endurance without guaranteed vindication

“Politics is a strong and slow boring of hard boards.”

— Max Weber, Politics as a Vocation (1919), Scott Horton translation. Source and attribution

The metaphor rejects both administrative passivity and the fantasy that moral intensity automatically produces political results. Durable change requires organization, repeated compromise and attention to consequences; the board resists regardless of the actor’s sincerity. Weber’s formulation can support reformism, but it does not logically rule out rupture. A revolutionary strategy also needs the unglamorous work of building institutions capable of surviving the moment of rupture.

sections.title: French usage: bon, je vais te laisser
sections.content:
Bon, je vais te laisser is a natural way to end a conversation: roughly “right, I should let you go” or “I’ll leave you to it.” It usually signals consideration for the other person rather than literal abandonment.

  • Bon, je vais te laisser, j’ai encore deux trucs à finir.
    Right, I should let you go; I still have a couple of things to finish.
  • Je vais vous laisser, merci encore et bonne journée.
    I’ll let you get on; thanks again, and have a good day.

Bon, je te laisse is more familiar and slightly brisker; je vais vous laisser is neutral and polite. Add a reason or closing formula when you want to avoid sounding abrupt. Do not confuse it with je te laisse faire, which means “I’ll let you handle it.” The Académie française records je vous laisse / je dois vous laisser specifically as formulas for taking leave. Académie française via CNRTL

sections.title: Music corner
sections.content: Three deliberately separated lanes: a short orchestral movement, foreground hard bop and a Mediterranean vocal song.

items.label: Classical
items.piece: Florence Price — Symphony No. 1 in E minor: III. “Juba Dance”
items.description: A deliberate 3:42 short-form slot after several long orchestral works. Price keeps a recurring dance idea immediately legible while moving it through syncopated strings, woodwind interjections and heavier brass punctuation. The movement is self-contained rather than an excerpt that depends on twenty minutes of preparation; it tests whether compact orchestral writing can deliver the melodic return and colouristic development you usually value in larger forms.

items.label: Jazz
items.piece: Roy Hargrove Quintet — “Strasbourg / St. Denis” — live
items.description: An eight-minute performance built around a strong trumpet-and-alto hook, a firm backbeat and solos that remain tied to the tune’s harmonic and rhythmic identity. The arrangement accumulates energy without becoming texturally messy, then earns its return to the main theme. This is foreground jazz rather than atmospheric trio writing, but its clarity and directed arc make it a better test than another groove track whose interest is mostly timbral.

items.label: Other
items.piece: Yasmin Levy — “Una Noche Más” — official video
items.description: A vocal-led Spanish-language song with a clear minor-key melody, restrained opening and a steadily enlarged arrangement of piano, guitar, bass and percussion. Levy’s delivery is dramatic, but the drama is supported by harmonic direction and a defined climax rather than treated as the whole point. It tests an emotionally direct Mediterranean vocal lane adjacent to the Silvana Estrada result, with more weight and development than the recent neutral singer-songwriter picks.

sections.title: Unrelated fact: Paris once put the metre into the street
sections.content:
Between 1796 and 1797, the French Academy of Sciences installed 16 marble metre standards around Paris so that shopkeepers and residents could directly compare rulers and goods with the new revolutionary unit. Measurement reform was not achieved merely by issuing a legal definition; the state had to make the unfamiliar length physically inspectable in ordinary public space.

Only two of those public standards survive. The one under the arcade at 36 rue de Vaugirard, opposite the Luxembourg Palace, remains in its original position. It is a small piece of infrastructure from the period when a universal abstract standard still needed to be taught through a literal groove in stone. NIST historical note

sections.title: Puzzle: the three-colour Ellsberg urn
sections.content:
An urn contains 90 balls:

  • exactly 30 are red;
  • the other 60 are black or yellow, but you are not told the split.

One ball will be drawn. First choose between:

  • A: win €100 if it is red;
  • B: win €100 if it is black.

Now make a separate choice between:

  • C: win €100 if it is red or yellow;
  • D: win €100 if it is black or yellow.

Many people choose A over B, because red has a known probability of one third, and then choose D over C, because black-or-yellow has a known probability of two thirds.

Question: are those two choices jointly rational? Try to assign subjective probabilities to red, black and yellow that justify both before reading further.

The difficulty is that A versus B depends only on red versus black. C versus D adds the same “win on yellow” outcome to both bets, so Savage’s sure-thing principle says the ranking should not reverse. Yet the common A/D pattern expresses a stable preference for known risk over unknown composition—ambiguity aversion—rather than an arithmetic mistake. The puzzle is whether rational-choice theory should prohibit that preference or expand beyond a single subjective probability distribution. Daniel Ellsberg’s 1961 paper
